Abide in the Vine
a-bīd´ ĭn thē vīn
v. phrase (the believer's continuance in Christ as a branch in the stock; rendering Greek meno en emoi)
Abide, Old English abīdan, to wait, remain; the Greek meno is to stay, to lodge, to keep on remaining. The vine is Israel's oldest self-image, and the Lord takes it over in the upper room.

Biblical Definition

“Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me” (John 15:4); “I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5). The alternative is stated without softening: “If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered” (John 15:6). The promise attached is prayer: “If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you” (John 15:7). Israel had been the vine that failed (Isa 5:1–7; Psa 80:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines abide as to rest, or dwell; to continue permanently or in the same state; to remain, to be firm and immovable.

expand to see more

ABIDE, v.i. To rest, or dwell.

2. To tarry or stay for a short time.

3. To continue permanently or in the same state; to be firm and immovable.

4. To remain, to continue.

Key Scripture

John 15:4 — "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me."

John 15:5 — "I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing."

John 15:6 — "If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned."

John 15:7 — "If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you."

John 15:16 — "Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you."

Modern Corruption

Abiding is made a mood to be maintained, and the figure is a branch that is either joined to the stock or is firewood.

expand to see more

Abiding has become one of the vaguest words in devotional English — a warm interior condition, achieved by quiet mornings and lost by busy ones, so that the Christian spends his life trying to get back into a feeling. The Greek is meno, to stay put, and the figure is horticultural rather than emotional. A branch does not abide by concentrating; it abides by not being cut off, and its abiding is visible in exactly one way, which the passage names four times: fruit. Verse 7 adds the second evidence, that His words abide in the disciple, which is a matter of what he knows and obeys rather than what he feels.

The clause everyone quotes is without me ye can do nothing, and it is usually softened to mean that things go better with prayer. The sentence has no such margin. A severed branch does not underperform; it dies, and its most vigorous appearance is the last of the sap it took with it. That is the doctrine of dependence at its sharpest, and it is spoken to apostles on the night before the crucifixion — men about to do more than any Christians since, and told in advance that their capacity was zero.

Verse 6 is the hard one and has been read as a threat of losing salvation. The chapter's own answer is verse 16: ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain — the same verb, meno. The branch that is taken away is the branch that never had life in it, the professing attachment with no sap crossing the join; Judas had left the room a few verses earlier, and the disciples had watched a branch be removed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek meno (G3306), to remain, abide, continue; ampelos (G288), vine; klema (G2814), branch; karpos (G2590), fruit; kathairo (G2508), to purge, prune.

expand to see more

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, remain; John 15:4–7, 15:9–10, 15:16, 1 John 2:6, 2:28, 3:24.

Greek ampelos (G288) — vine; John 15:1, 15:4–5, Revelation 14:18; klema (G2814), branch; John 15:2, 15:4–6.

Greek kathairo (G2508) — to prune, purge; John 15:2, with the wordplay on katharoi, clean, in 15:3.

Usage

"“As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself” — cannot, not merely will not."

"“Without me ye can do nothing” — said to apostles, the night before the cross."

"“That your fruit should remain” — the same verb as abide."
